rationale: The investigators compared 10 people with probable DLB, 76 with probable Alzheimer disease and 17 with Parkinson dementia. The groups completed cognitive tests, with fluctuating Parkinson participants tested during the on phase. Hallucinations appear in the description of DLB. The comparison concerns cognitive performance and does not quantify repeated visual experiences or assign a food exposure.

Seventy-five people with mild dementia received clinical and PET-based classifications. About 35% differed between approaches, with agreement kappa 0.39. The 14 people clinically classified with Lewy body dementia included 29% with a discordant PET classification. Spontaneous visual hallucinations were a diagnostic feature considered with other signs. The measured contrast is between classification methods, and there is no dried fig or episode-frequency comparison.

The experiment compared isolated drug enantiomers in a primate model and rated movement outcomes and observed psychosis-like behaviors during levodopa testing. The R enantiomer affected the disabling subset of the behavior measure without a significant change in the duration of any such behavior. These observer ratings do not establish what the animals saw or how often people with Parkinson disease hallucinate. Dried fig intake was not studied.

Twenty-three people with Parkinson disease and 27 controls had baseline PET. Six Parkinson participants were later diagnosed with dementia. Lower glucose metabolism in visual association and posterior cingulate regions was associated with subsequent dementia. The discussion cites hallucination work, while the measured longitudinal event was dementia diagnosis. The dataset does not test a food exposure or separate visual hallucination recurrence.

The brain-bank analysis included 56 pathology-confirmed Parkinson cases. Dementia classification drew on recorded clinical courses, with visual hallucinations and fluctuating confusion noted as clinical context. The reported associations concern combined Lewy and Alzheimer-type pathology and dementia. Twenty-three cases had been partially assessed in a prior cohort analysis. The study provides no food-linked symptom change or matched event-count endpoint.

The review discusses degeneration outside the nigrostriatal system and how experimental models reproduce motor and nonmotor features. Differences in model pathology and experimental outcomes limit translation. The reviewed measurements give no clinical visual episode-frequency result linked to dried figs.

The review discusses visual, auditory, tactile and olfactory experiences separately, contrasts early untreated observations with longitudinal treated cohorts, and surveys pharmacologic and disease-related risk factors. Reported prevalence estimates come from earlier studies with different designs. The review adds no independent participant series or ingredient comparison.

The review examines receptor assembly, experimental probes and receptor contributions to dopaminergic signaling. Parkinson relevance is mechanistic. Receptor activity does not measure patient visual hallucination recurrence, and the material does not compare culinary fig intake.

This report describes parkinsonism with a glucocerebrosidase mutation and discusses observations in other Gaucher-associated cases. Visual hallucinations in the discussion concern earlier reports. The case supplies no repeat measure of visual events or contrast by food exposure.

A person initially evaluated for pure autonomic failure reported visual hallucinations by the second follow-up year and worsening by the fourth year, as cognitive and motor findings evolved. The authors subsequently considered probable DLB. Imaging and autonomic measurements track different components of the course. The visual account records timing and perceived worsening with no comparable episode-count windows or food intervention.

The paper reviews SNCA dosage, expression and familial parkinsonism. It summarizes visual and other hallucinations in earlier kindreds as part of differing clinical phenotypes. Those case descriptions add no independent intake comparison or visual event rate in this review.

The article compares structural and molecular imaging approaches across dementias. It treats dopamine transporter measurements and related scans as aids to differential diagnosis. The review supplies no intervention-specific clinical visual episode measurement or evidence about dried figs.

The investigators analyzed 41 people with probable or possible DLB. They compared 21 acute with 20 chronic presentations and separately grouped the initial complaints by cognitive features. Table 3 summarizes the distribution of symptoms within initial and subsequent symptom categories. The method describes onset and symptom mix rather than the number of recurring visual episodes per person. No dietary intervention was studied.

The report describes three people initially assessed for an Alzheimer-type presentation with abnormal dopamine transporter imaging. One case had uncontrolled visual hallucinations without evident motor parkinsonism at examination. Another described brief experiences closer to misperceptions. The paper illustrates uncertainty in clinical classification. It does not follow visual episode rates under dried fig exposure.

The case traces early-onset parkinsonism before recognition of Gaucher disease and describes multiple treatment changes over follow-up. Benign visual hallucinations are reported in the discussion of levodopa withdrawal, along with loss of response. The text does not identify an independent visual event rate, isolate a drug effect from disease course or measure dried fig intake.
